title: Stop Calling Them Soft Skills
paragraphs: Last month, a recruiter in Monterrey told me that her company had received six hundred applications for a single marketing post. Almost all the candidates had the right degree and the right software. What she was looking for, she said, was something harder to find: somebody who could disagree with a colleague without starting a feud. 'We can teach the programs,' she sighed. 'We cannot teach the character.'

I have heard this complaint in many offices, and it always arrives with the same label attached: soft skills. Listening, negotiating, explaining a problem clearly, admitting a mistake. The adjective is the trouble. It implies that these abilities are decorative, pleasant extras to be added once the real work has been done. Anyone who has watched a project collapse because two departments refused to talk to each other knows how mistaken that is.

Part of the confusion comes from our schools. Examinations measure what is easy to measure: dates, formulas, spelling. Rarely does a student receive a mark for noticing that a teammate is struggling, or for persuading a sceptical audience. What is not measured is, in practice, not valued, and what is not valued is not taught. It is hardly surprising that employers later complain about the very gaps that the system has created.

Some will argue that these capacities are simply personality, fixed early and impossible to change. Although temperament certainly plays a part, the evidence points elsewhere. Anyone who has learned to speak in public after years of terror, or to give honest feedback without wounding, has experienced the opposite. These are techniques, and like all techniques they improve with practice, feedback and, above all, humility.

Calling them hard would not solve everything, but language shapes priorities. A manager who says that a candidate is strong on the technical side but weak on the soft side has, almost without noticing, ranked the two. Imagine instead a job advertisement that listed 'resolving conflict' next to 'advanced spreadsheets' and offered a salary linked to both. The message to applicants, and to universities, would be unmistakable.

Employers are not blameless either. Job advertisements routinely demand 'excellent communication skills' and 'a team player', yet interviews rarely test either quality. Candidates are asked to describe their strengths in abstract terms, which rewards those who are good at talking about themselves rather than those who are good at working with others. It is a small irony that the process of selection often ignores precisely what the employer says it wants.

There is a gendered dimension too, which deserves a sentence of its own. Work that involves care, mediation and emotional attention has traditionally been performed by women and, not coincidentally, has traditionally been paid less. Relabelling it as 'soft' makes that old habit sound like common sense. Names are never neutral; they carry a verdict.

I am not suggesting that we invent a fashionable new term every time a fashionable old one grows tired. I am suggesting something simpler. The next time somebody praises a colleague for being 'good with people', ask what, precisely, that person does that others do not. The answer will almost certainly describe a skill, one that required effort to build and that the whole team depends on every single day.

questions.explain_es: Ella afirma: 'We can teach the programs... We cannot teach the character.'

title: The Maths of the Phantom Jam
paragraphs: Most drivers have experienced it: a motorway slows to a crawl, brake lights glow for several kilometres, and then, without warning, the road clears. There is no accident, no roadworks and no obvious obstacle. The jam has simply dissolved, leaving everyone to wonder what it was ever for. Traffic physicists have a name for such events. They call them phantom jams, and they have shown that these jams can arise from nothing more than ordinary human behaviour.

The mechanism is surprisingly simple. Imagine a dense line of cars moving at a similar speed. One driver brakes slightly, perhaps because a lorry has changed lane ahead. The driver behind reacts a fraction of a second later and brakes a little harder than necessary, to be safe. The next driver does the same. Each reaction is small, but the effect accumulates, and a short way back along the line a car comes to a complete stop.

The result is a wave that travels backwards. Although the cars themselves move forwards, the region of stopped traffic drifts in the opposite direction, rather like a ripple moving against the current. Drivers enter it, wait, and leave it, while the jam itself continues to move backwards at a steady pace. A frustrating consequence is that the cause of the jam, the original touch of the brake, may be several kilometres and several minutes behind you by the time you reach it.

In 2008, a group of Japanese researchers put this theory to a striking test. They asked about twenty drivers to circle a track at a steady speed and an even distance from one another. At first, the traffic flowed smoothly. Within a few minutes, however, small fluctuations grew, and a jam appeared on a track with no bottleneck at all. The experiment is often cited because it makes the invisible visible.

The same principle applies to many other systems. Queues at a supermarket, crowds leaving a stadium and even the flow of data across a network can behave in comparable ways, with small disturbances growing into large delays. For this reason, the mathematics of traffic has attracted the interest of researchers who have never driven a car for a living, including specialists in biology and computer science.

These findings have practical implications. Because the problem lies in how drivers respond, rather than in the road, widening a motorway may not cure it. Some researchers recommend that drivers keep a larger gap and avoid sharp braking, so that they absorb disturbances instead of passing them on. Others look to technology: cars with adaptive cruise control can, in principle, smooth the flow by reacting more gently than people do.

It would be wrong to claim that the phantom jam explains all congestion. Roadworks, accidents and simple overcrowding remain the main causes in most cities, and they cannot be solved by politeness. Still, there is something instructive in the idea that a crowd of reasonable individuals, each acting sensibly, can produce an outcome that nobody wants. Traffic is not only an engineering problem; it is also a small lesson in how groups behave.
glossary: control de crucero adaptativo (mantiene la distancia con el auto de delante)

title: The Archivist of City Sounds
paragraphs: Nkechi Eze can identify a London bus route with her eyes closed. The pitch of the engine, the sigh of the doors and the rattle of a loose panel are, to her, as distinctive as a face. For nine years, Eze, a Nigerian-British sound recordist, has been collecting the everyday noises of cities, from the call of a market trader in Peckham to the evening generators of her grandmother's street in Enugu. Her archive now holds more than eleven thousand recordings.

The project began almost by accident. Eze was working as a radio technician when a veteran colleague retired and mentioned, in passing, that the old sound of the printing presses nearby had disappeared with the last newspaper. 'Nobody recorded it,' she says. 'Photographs were taken, articles were written, but the actual sound is gone.' That remark stayed with her. A week later she bought a small recorder and began walking.

Her method is deliberate. She records at the same location at different hours and in different seasons, noting the weather, the date and the approximate number of people nearby. Each file is stored with a short description, written, as she puts it, 'for somebody who has never been here'. The result is less a collection of noises than a diary of places, in which a quiet street at dawn may matter as much as a festival.

Some friends find the work puzzling. Why preserve the sound of a ticket machine that will probably be replaced next year? Eze's answer is that replacement is precisely the point. 'Every object you take for granted will become strange,' she says. 'A century from now, someone will want to know what a Tuesday morning sounded like in our time, and we shall have left them nothing.' She speaks without drama, as though stating the obvious.

The archive has found unexpected uses. A film studio paid a modest fee, around two hundred pounds, to license recordings of a vanished railway station. Linguists have asked for samples of street conversations, with names removed, to study how accents change from one district to another. A group of elderly residents in Enugu wept when they heard the generators of their youth played back in a library.

Funding remains the main difficulty. Eze works part-time as a technician to pay her rent, and most of the archive is maintained in her spare hours. She has applied to several foundations, with limited success. 'People understand a painting,' she says. 'A recording of a Tuesday is harder to sell.' Even so, she is not discouraged, and she has trained two volunteers who now record in Lagos and Manchester.

Asked what she listens to when she is off duty, Eze laughs and admits that the answer is silence, or something close to it. Then she pauses. 'There is no such thing as complete silence in a city,' she says. 'Even at three in the morning, there is a refrigerator humming somewhere, and somebody has to write it down.'
glossary: zumbar, emitir un sonido continuo bajo

title: The Tyranny of the Cliffhanger
paragraphs: The cliffhanger is almost as old as storytelling itself. In the tradition of the Thousand and One Nights, Scheherazade postpones her execution by stopping each tale at the most exciting moment, so that the king must wait until the following night to hear the ending. In the nineteenth century, Charles Dickens published many of his novels in monthly or weekly instalments, and readers in the street reportedly begged for news of what would happen next. The device works, and it has always worked.

What has changed is its function. For Scheherazade, the suspense was a matter of survival; for Dickens, a method of selling magazines. Today it has become something stranger: a habit. On streaming platforms, the next episode begins automatically a few seconds after the previous one ends, and the final scene of almost every episode is designed to make stopping feel like a small act of cruelty. Rarely does a series now allow its viewers to finish an episode satisfied.

I would not object if this were simply a matter of craft. A well-placed cliffhanger can be thrilling, and some of the finest television of the past twenty years depends on it. My concern is that the technique has been separated from the story and transformed into a retention strategy. A twist is no longer included because the plot requires it, but because a dashboard shows that audiences tend to leave at minute forty. Narrative is bending to fit the metric.

The consequences are visible on screen. Plots are stretched to fill ten episodes that could have filled six. Characters make absurd decisions so that a problem can be postponed. Mysteries are introduced with great ceremony and abandoned without explanation, since the writers never needed an answer, only a question. Viewers sense the trick, and the more often they are cheated, the less they care.

Nor is the damage limited to quality. A story that ends in suspense leaves a feeling of unfinished business, and that feeling is precisely what keeps us pressing the button. We tell ourselves that we are enjoying the programme, yet many of us close the laptop at one in the morning with a vague sense that we have been managed rather than entertained. Pleasure, properly speaking, includes satisfaction, and satisfaction requires an ending.

This is not an argument against serial storytelling. Some of the most beautiful narratives ever created unfold slowly, and the best of them trust their audience enough to let each chapter be complete in itself. A season can build towards a larger question while still giving viewers a reason to be content at the end of every hour. Writers who can do both deserve our attention and, frankly, our gratitude.

Perhaps the simplest remedy lies with the viewer. The platforms will not change their settings voluntarily, but we can change ours. Turn off the automatic playback. Allow the credits to roll. Let a story rest for a day, and notice how much more it lingers. The best endings, like the best silences, are those we choose to enjoy rather than those we are rushed through.
glossary: entrega (de una serie, de una novela por capítulos)

title: A Wedding in Salta
focus: Narrative tenses, inversion and cleft sentences
paragraphs: The invitation had specified that the ceremony would begin at six, and by seven nobody in the garden had so much as looked at a watch. Lucrecia stood beside the empanada table with a glass of wine she did not want, watching her cousin's relatives arrive in slow, noisy groups. Salta in March was warm and generous, and the hills behind the house turned orange as the sun dropped. It was exactly the sort of evening on which families told lies without noticing.

She had come from Córdoba on a night bus, rehearsing what she would say if her uncle Ernesto approached her. Eleven years earlier, he had refused to lend her father the money that might have saved the small shop, and her father had never recovered from the disappointment. At the funeral, Ernesto had cried more loudly than anyone. Lucrecia had not forgiven him either for the refusal or for the performance.

He did approach her, of course, shortly after the first dance. He was heavier now, his moustache entirely white, and he carried two plates of food as though they were a peace offering. 'Eat,' he said. 'You look like your mother.' She almost laughed. It was the type of remark that was impossible to answer politely and impossible to answer rudely, and he knew it.

They sat at a table at the edge of the garden, where the music was only a murmur. For a while they discussed nothing, the weather, her studies, the price of bus tickets, which had risen again. Then Ernesto put down his fork. 'Your father never told you why I said no,' he said. It was not a question. Lucrecia felt her whole body grow still.

What followed was brief. The shop, Ernesto explained, had been failing for years, and the loan would simply have buried two families instead of one. He had calculated, in the cold way of a man who has spent his life with accounts, that a refusal would save his brother's house even if it cost him his brother's affection. 'Your father understood,' he said. 'He did not forgive me, but he understood.' The house, she remembered, had indeed been kept.

She wanted to believe that this was a lie, a convenient story assembled over a decade. Yet the details were too exact: the dates, the sums, even the name of the lawyer. Nobody invents that much to defend himself. Nor did he ask for anything. He simply folded his napkin and returned to the dance floor, leaving her with a plate she had not touched and a memory that suddenly had a different shape.

Later that night, as the band played a slow zamba and couples drifted across the grass, Lucrecia found herself walking towards him. She did not say she forgave him. She asked him instead to dance, and he accepted with the same solemn courtesy with which one accepts a gift too large to be thanked aloud. Above them, the hills had vanished into darkness, and the stars were beginning to show.
glossary: ofrenda de paz, gesto de reconciliación

questions.explain_es: Narra que no lo había perdonado 'either for the refusal or for the performance'.

questions.explain_es: Dice que el préstamo 'would simply have buried two families instead of one'.

options: He wanted to protect his brother's house
He had no money of his own
He disliked his brother's shop
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: calculó que negarse salvaría la casa de su hermano 'even if it cost him his brother's affection'; la casa, de hecho, se conservó.

questions.q: How does Lucrecia seem to feel at the end of the story?
options: Satisfied that she has proved him wrong
Furious and eager to leave
Moved and ready to reconcile
questions.explain_es: Actitud: lo invita a bailar, 'a gift too large to be thanked aloud'; no dice que lo perdona, pero el gesto muestra reconciliación.

questions.q: Why does the author mention that the details Ernesto gave were 'too exact'?
options: To suggest that Ernesto rehearsed the speech
To show that Lucrecia now finds his story credible

questions.explain_es: Propósito: la exactitud (fechas, sumas, el nombre del abogado) lleva a Lucrecia a creerle: 'Nobody invents that much to defend himself'.

questions.q: How does the opening description of the evening help the story?
options: It shows that the family is wealthy
It prepares the theme of hidden truths
It explains why the wedding was late
questions.explain_es: Estructura: la frase final del primer párrafo ('families told lies without noticing') anticipa el tema del secreto que se revela después.

options: size
meaning

title: Youth Employment Survey: Key Findings
topic: Young people and the labour market
focus: Formal report language and data description
paragraphs: ## 1. Background

This extract summarises the principal results of a survey of 1,200 young people aged between eighteen and twenty-nine, conducted across four cities in Ecuador (Quito, Guayaquil, Cuenca and Ambato) between March and May. Respondents were selected so as to reflect the age, gender and educational profile of each city. The survey was commissioned by a regional development agency and carried out by an independent research team.
## 2. Employment status

Just under half of those surveyed (47 per cent) reported being in paid employment only, while 21 per cent were studying full time and 18 per cent were both working and studying. The remaining 14 per cent were neither employed nor in education. This last group, often described as inactive, was disproportionately female and included many respondents who were caring for relatives.

Among those in paid work, almost four in ten had no written contract. The proportion was highest among respondents who had not completed secondary school (61 per cent) and lowest among university graduates (22 per cent). Median monthly earnings were reported as 480 dollars, with a pronounced difference between respondents with and without a degree.

Differences between cities were also apparent. Guayaquil recorded the highest share of respondents in paid employment (52 per cent), while Cuenca had the largest proportion of full-time students (27 per cent). The authors attribute this partly to the presence of several universities in Cuenca, although they stress that the sample for each city is too small to support firm conclusions about local labour markets.

Job satisfaction was measured on a five-point scale. The average score was 3.2, with respondents in jobs related to their studies reporting markedly higher satisfaction than those in unrelated work. Women and men gave similar scores overall, but women were more likely to report that they had been asked questions about marriage or children during selection interviews, a practice that is prohibited by national legislation.
## 3. Expectations and barriers

Respondents were asked to name the greatest obstacle to finding stable employment. The most frequent answer, given by 38 per cent, was a lack of work experience; the cost of transport to interviews was mentioned by 17 per cent, and a similar share referred to age or gender discrimination. Only 9 per cent cited a lack of qualifications, which suggests that the problem is perceived more as access than as preparation.

Optimism was nevertheless widespread. Some 62 per cent expected their situation to improve within two years, although this proportion fell to 41 per cent among those who had been unemployed for more than a year. Researchers caution that expectations of this kind are known to be unreliable and should not be treated as forecasts.
## 4. Limitations and recommendations

The survey was conducted in urban areas only, so the results cannot be generalised to rural populations, where informal work is likely to be more common. Self-reported income is also subject to error. With these reservations, the authors recommend that municipal programmes prioritise paid internships, subsidised transport for job seekers and clearer information about contract rights, since each of these measures addresses a barrier identified by a substantial share of respondents.

title: The Price of a Fast Parcel
topic: Delivery work and the gig economy
paragraphs: At eleven on a Friday night in Bogotá, Andrés Molina is still on his motorbike, one eye on the road and the other on the phone attached to his handlebars. He has delivered twenty-three orders since noon. When the app offers him another, he has fifteen seconds to accept; a refusal lowers his rating, and a lower rating, he says, means fewer good jobs. 'You do not really decide,' he says. 'The phone decides, and you obey.'

Molina is one of tens of thousands of couriers who work for delivery platforms in Colombia's cities. The companies describe them as independent partners who choose their hours freely, and they emphasise the flexibility of the arrangement. In more than thirty interviews carried out for this investigation, however, couriers described a system in which flexibility exists mainly on paper. Those who decline orders, or who log off during busy periods, reported being offered fewer jobs the following week.

Earnings are harder to establish than the companies' public statements suggest. Molina showed us his records for a typical week. He earned roughly 620,000 pesos in fourteen-hour days, from which he subtracted around 150,000 for petrol, 40,000 for maintenance and a monthly instalment on a bike he is still paying for. The total is not negligible, but, as he points out, nothing in the figures accounts for the days he is injured or ill.

Safety is a persistent concern. According to several riders, the pressure to meet delivery times encourages dangerous manoeuvres, especially in rain. One courier showed us a scar on his forearm from a fall on a wet road. The platforms offer limited accident insurance, but riders say the process of claiming it is slow and the cover excludes the first days of treatment. A company representative said the insurance 'meets the requirements of the law' and declined to answer further questions.

The legal status of these workers is at the heart of the dispute. If they are independent, the companies owe them no holiday pay, no contributions to a pension and no minimum wage. If they are in practice employees, all of that changes. Courts in several countries have begun to examine the question, reaching different conclusions, and the Colombian authorities have said they are studying proposals. Nobody has yet offered a final answer.

It would be too simple to present the riders merely as victims. Several told us they value the speed with which they can start earning, particularly in a city where formal jobs are scarce. A student named Paola Rincón said the work had paid for her first year at university. Yet even she hesitated when asked whether she would recommend it to a friend. 'For a while, yes,' she said. 'Not as a life.'

The deeper question is what customers owe the people who bring their dinner. Convenience has a cost, and it is not always printed on the receipt. Until the rules are clearer, those who use the apps might at least ask what the price of a fast parcel really includes, and who is paying the part that is missing.

title: On Being Wrong in Public
paragraphs: Few experiences are as uncomfortable as discovering, in front of other people, that one was mistaken. The heat rises in the face, the voice grows thin, and the mind searches desperately for a way to turn the error into something else: a misunderstanding, a slip, a question of wording. We spend a surprising amount of energy avoiding these moments, and I suspect we pay a higher price for that avoidance than for the errors themselves.

The reason is not hard to find. In most workplaces and schools, being wrong is treated as a sign of low ability. Were mistakes seen as information, people would report them early; as they are seen as failures, people hide them until they grow. Some of the most expensive disasters in industry, medicine and aviation have been traced to a junior employee who noticed a problem and said nothing, for fear of looking foolish.

It is instructive to compare this with the culture of science at its best. A scientist who publishes a result and later finds it to be false is expected to say so, plainly, and the correction becomes part of the record. This does not always happen, and egos exist in laboratories like anywhere else. Nevertheless, the principle is admirable: no one is exempt from error, so the only fair question is how quickly it is acknowledged.

In everyday life the equivalent is the sentence 'I was wrong', which is remarkably difficult to pronounce. Notice how often we substitute weaker versions. 'Mistakes were made' avoids naming the person who made them. 'I see where you are coming from' concedes nothing. 'Well, it depends' pretends that the original claim was cautious all along. Each of these evasions protects the speaker slightly, and damages the conversation considerably.

Why, then, is the direct admission so rare? Partly because it is risky. In an argument, we fear that acknowledging one mistake will be taken as an admission of general weakness. Yet experience suggests the opposite. The colleagues I trust most are precisely those who say, without ceremony, 'I got that wrong, thank you for correcting me'. Their confidence does not depend on being right, and so it is not threatened when they are not.

None of this is easy for those who grew up being rewarded for correct answers. Perfectionism can be remarkably persistent, and it is encouraged by social media, where every opinion is permanent and every retraction is a spectacle. A teacher of mine, a quiet woman from Quito, used to begin each term by announcing that she expected to make three mistakes a week and would be grateful if we pointed them out. Her classroom was the most relaxed I have ever known.

If I could change one habit in public life, it would be this: to make correction ordinary. A culture that expects errors will spot them sooner and repair them more cheaply. And an individual who can say 'I was wrong' without flinching has acquired something rarer than being right, a mind that remains open, and therefore capable of becoming right in the future.

title: Gardening the Reef
paragraphs: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species. This extraordinary concentration of life depends on a partnership: tiny algae live inside the tissues of the coral, providing it with food through photosynthesis, while the coral offers shelter. The arrangement works well until the water grows too warm. Under heat stress, corals expel their algae, turn pale and, if the stress continues, starve. This process is known as bleaching.

As ocean temperatures have risen, bleaching has become more frequent in many regions, and some reefs have little time to recover between episodes. Scientists agree that the long-term solution is to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Yet that solution is slow, and some reefs may not survive long enough to benefit from it. This is the context in which an unusual form of conservation has developed, one that resembles gardening more than the traditional protection of wilderness.

Coral gardening begins with a fragment. Divers break small pieces from healthy colonies, taking care not to harm the parent, and attach them to ropes or frames in underwater nurseries. In the calm, well-lit water, the fragments grow quickly, sometimes several centimetres a year. Once they are large enough, they are fixed with cement or small clips to damaged parts of a reef, where they may develop into new colonies. The technique has been used most widely with branching Caribbean species such as staghorn coral.

Results have been encouraging. In several locations, reefs that were once covered in rubble now support fish, crabs and young corals again. Local communities have also benefited: in some places, fishermen and former tourist guides have been trained as divers and technicians, and receive modest wages for tending the nurseries. Projects of this kind tend to attract tourism, which in turn provides funding, though that is not a guaranteed result.

Critics raise legitimate objections. Planting fragments is labour-intensive, and the cost per hectare is high compared with other conservation measures. More fundamentally, if the water continues to warm, transplanted corals will bleach just like their neighbours. Gardening can therefore treat a symptom but cannot cure the cause. There is also a genetic concern: if all the new colonies are cloned from a few fragments, the population will lack the diversity that helps species adapt.

Researchers are responding to these problems in various ways. Some select fragments from colonies that survived hot summers, hoping to pass on their tolerance. Others raise corals from larvae collected after spawning, which produces genetically varied offspring. These strategies remain experimental, and nobody can yet say how effective they will be over decades. What is clear is that the work requires patience and willingness to learn from failure.

Most of the people involved are careful not to oversell their work. Coral gardening, they say, buys time; it does not replace the reduction of emissions. But time is exactly what many reefs need. A gardener does not plant a tree believing that it alone will restore a forest. She plants it because it is something that can be done today, and because the forest, one day, may be grateful.
